title: Factoring Polynomials
summary: Factoring reverses multiplication: pull out the GCF, factor by grouping, factor trinomials, and recognize special forms (difference of squares, perfect-square trinomials, sum/difference of cubes). Factoring is the key to solving polynomial equations.

factor.plain: A multiplied piece of an expression.
factor.in_class: Factoring writes a polynomial as a product.

GCF.plain: Greatest common factor of all terms.

grouping.in_class: Group, factor each pair, then factor the shared binomial.

trinomial.in_class: Find factors of $c$ that add to $b$.

perfect-square trinomial.plain: A trinomial that's a squared binomial.

leading coefficient.plain: The number in front of the highest power.
leading coefficient.in_class: Affects the trinomial method (a≠1 needs AC method).

concept_sections.heading: Greatest common factor
concept_sections.explanation: Always factor out the GCF first — the largest monomial dividing every term. It simplifies whatever technique comes next.
math_steps: Find the largest common numeric and variable factor.
Divide it out of every term.

concept_sections.heading: Factoring by grouping
concept_sections.explanation: For four terms, group into two pairs, factor each pair, and if a common binomial appears, factor it out.
math_steps: Factor the GCF from each pair.

concept_sections.heading: Trinomials $x^2+bx+c$
concept_sections.explanation: Find two numbers that multiply to $c$ and add to $b$; they give the binomial factors $(x+p)(x+q)$. When the leading coefficient isn't 1, use the AC method.

concept_sections.heading: Special forms
concept_sections.explanation: Recognize $a^2-b^2=(a+b)(a-b)$, perfect squares $a^2\pm2ab+b^2=(a\pm b)^2$, and cubes $a^3\pm b^3$. Spotting these skips trial and error.
math_steps: Check for a difference of squares.

concept_sections.heading: A general strategy
concept_sections.explanation: Factor completely: GCF first, then match a special form, then trinomial or grouping, and finally check that each factor is fully factored.

real_world_examples.title: Solving by the zero-product rule
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Factoring turns $x^2-5x+6=0$ into $(x-2)(x-3)=0$, revealing the roots.

real_world_examples.title: Simplifying a rational expression
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Factoring top and bottom lets common factors cancel.

real_world_examples.title: Optimizing dimensions
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Factoring an area polynomial exposes the dimensions that make it zero or maximal.
